posts.author: Mira Ling
posts.headline: Co-Founder & CPO @ Ambitology.com | Building career and opening for a tech job?
posts.text: AI job titles are multiplying—and that can make it harder to see where you fit. A recent r/developersIndia discussion came from a 2026 graduate weighing SDE-1 and forward-deployed roles after experience across software, full stack, product, and ML research. The Friday thread had 19 upvotes and 13 comments when I checked. A newer Sunday question from a Python full-stack developer choosing between GenAI Engineer, ML Engineer, and other paths had 2 votes and 3 comments. Those are community conversations, not proof of hiring demand. You don’t need to choose your whole future based on a title. Start with the work: • Find the problems a role asks you to solve. • Pick one project that shows relevant skills in action. • Be ready to explain what you built, how you checked it, and what you’d improve. A title can point you toward a door; your work shows what you bring through it. As a founder, I believe career decisions get clearer when you can see how your skills connect to possible next roles. Ambitology Skill Graph helps connect learning and skills with roles that may fit. https://lnkd.in/g4wUvBUB If you’re exploring AI work, which role family feels closest to your strengths?

posts.text: Robots are about to work next to millions of people. Somebody has to write the code that keeps them safe. 🤖🛡️ Our Compass team at Amazon Robotics is growing, and we're hiring software engineers in Pasadena, CA. Compass is building the certified safety foundation for Amazon's entire robotics fleet. We work alongside the inventors of control barrier functions on a universal approach to safe autonomy. It has to work across mobile robots, manipulators, mobile manipulators, and even legged and dynamically stable platforms. The goal: safety that never gets in the way of performance. We have two kinds of engineering roles open: ⚙️ Embedded Robotics SDE Take algorithms from our R&D team and turn them into production-grade, certifiable embedded software (think C++, MISRA/AUTOSAR-style standards, deterministic real-time execution). You'll own the library of safety-critical modules and carry it through the full certification lifecycle, from research prototype to certified product. 🔗 Robotics SDE, Safe Autonomy Own how Compass plugs into real robots. You'll design the abstractions and APIs that separate safety logic from hardware, connect with motion planning, perception, and safety-rated firmware, and build the simulation pipelines that prove it all works, at fleet scale. Both are open at the mid and senior levels. You might be a great fit if you: ✔️ Write C++ (or Rust) for real-time or embedded systems ✔️ Care about reliability, traceability, and doing things the right way ✔️ Enjoy working with research-minded teams on hard, unsolved problems ✔️ Want your code to sit between a robot and the people around it Bonus points for experience with ROS/ROS2, functional safety standards, control barrier functions, RTOS, or robot simulation. And if you don't tick every box, apply anyway. 📍 Pasadena, CA Interested? posts.text: Just hit 2,000 internship applications over three years. Freshman year me just spammed generic resumes and hoped for the best. Fast forward to now, and it turns out most standard advice is just pretty mid. Narrowing down 2,000 applications to three real takeaways: 𝟏. 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐚 𝐝𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐡𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐬. Waiting weeks for a referral usually means missing the review cap entirely. Checking daily boards and submitting within the first 24 hours lands your resume right at the top of the stack. 𝟐. 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐤𝐞𝐲 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐡𝐮𝐛𝐬. Show up, ask sharp questions, and get your resume onto internal event lists. Recruiters remember engaged faces, and they usually share direct hiring timelines or direct consideration links before the public rush. 𝟑. 𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐣𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐛𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞. Recruiters started reaching out directly once I stopped relying just on cold applications. Posting my hackathon projects on LinkedIn, breaking down my work, and having a personal website to show demos makes it clear what I can actually build. Mass applying gives you baseline reps, but personal branding is what actually gets eyes on your work. #swe #internships #wagmi

posts.text: Software Developer Job Postings Rise Despite AI Coding Automation. AI Can Write Code, But It Still Needs Adult Supervision. The Structural Shift in Tech Hiring: Seniority and AI Systems Engineering. Why AI is Driving Demand for Senior Developers. Software developers were supposed to be first in line for the AI guillotine. Yet, despite artificial intelligence now writing a third of all new code and automating routine programming tasks, US software developer job postings have ironically climbed nearly 15 percent since early 2025. The controversy is stark: the machines have not replaced the engineering department, they have simply redefined what an engineer actually does. This trend is a vital signal for chief technology officers, tech recruiters, and computer science graduates. As generative AI turns code generation into a cheap commodity, the market is aggressively rewarding developers who can review, integrate, and architect systems, proving that verifying code is now far more valuable than writing it. The current hiring rebound is highly concentrated. Employment data reveals that 71 percent of the recent increase in developer postings comes from senior roles, with a significant chunk explicitly requiring AI expertise. While overall postings remain below pre pandemic peaks, the demand for experienced talent is surging. Writing code is no longer the bottleneck for software teams. The new constraint is systems judgment. Companies are desperate for experienced architects who can oversee AI agents, wire generated code into complex legacy systems, and take accountability for the final product when the algorithm inevitably makes a mistake. Meanwhile, the entry level pipeline is collapsing. Hiring for early career software developers has plunged by roughly 20 percent since the generative AI boom began. The foundational junior tasks that historically served as a training ground for new graduates have been almost entirely automated. This creates a ticking time bomb for the tech industry. If companies refuse to hire and train junior developers today because an AI can do the basic work cheaper, they are virtually guaranteeing a catastrophic shortage of the very senior engineers they so desperately need a few years from now. HR, CTOs, COOs and CFOs - are you listening? Read more here: https://lnkd.in/g-RwfS4t

posts.headline: I Help Software Engineers land FAANG jobs | Ex-Microsoft, Ex-Amazon | Principal Engineer | Fractional Technical Advisor for Growth-Stage Startups
posts.text: Google opened 130 new senior-and-above US engineering roles last week. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Apple, Oracle, NVIDIA, and Netflix together posted 927 new core roles. They also closed 1,077. I track this every Monday now. The closes still outpace the opens. The market isn't hiring like 2021. It's swapping seats. Roles disappear, new ones show up with AI in the title, and a lot of senior people are stuck wondering where they fit. 334 of the 1,806 new US engineering roles I tracked this week were AI/ML. About 18%. Here's the part that surprised me. The median senior AI/ML base now starts at $174,000. Senior SWE starts at $168,100. At the top of the band, AI/ML is about $17K higher. So "learn AI" isn't a raise by itself. Landing higher in the band is. I spent years at Amazon, Microsoft, and Oracle, most recently as a Principal engineer, and I sat in a lot of loops. The people who cleared the top of the band weren't always the ones with the flashiest stack. They could explain what they owned, the tradeoffs they made, and why it mattered to the business. That's a skill. It can be practiced. If you're a senior engineer looking at one of these Big Tech or AI roles and you're not sure where you'd land, DM me "fit check." I'll tell you honestly whether coaching makes sense, and if it doesn't, I'll say so. (Postings show base pay only, not stock or bonus.)

posts.author: Alessandro Furlanetto
posts.headline: Technical Lead & Architect | AI‑Augmented SDLC | DevSecOps & Governance | Identity & Distributed Systems
posts.text: AI is killing junior software jobs. That's the narrative I've been hearing for months. Then I looked at the facts. Yes, employment among younger software developers in the US is below the 2022 peak. That's a signal worth watching carefully. But a 20% decline in hiring is not the same thing as the extinction of a profession. If companies hired 100 junior developers before and now hire 80, that's a market adjustment. Not a collapse. What I find particularly interesting is that Accenture, one of the world's most aggressive adopters and sellers of AI solutions, publicly stated that it plans to hire more entry-level talent in 2026 than it did in 2025. That's a curious strategy for a company that should, theoretically, understand AI-driven workforce disruption before most others. Perhaps we're looking at the wrong variable. We often describe a senior engineer as a junior engineer with more years of coding experience. I'm not convinced; a senior professional is not the person who remembers the most APIs, frameworks, or commands. A senior professional understands context. They: - identify the real problem. - navigate trade-offs. - make decisions under uncertainty. - own the consequences. AI is undoubtedly reducing the value of a great deal of routine technical work. What remains unproven is the assumption that routine technical work was the same thing as professional growth. Maybe AI isn't eliminating the path to expertise. Maybe it's eliminating some of the tasks we mistakenly confused with expertise. The real question isn't: "Who will do the work of junior developers?" The real question is: "How do we develop professional judgment in a world where execution is becoming almost free?" That is a much harder question. And probably the more important one. #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #SoftwareEngineering #Technology #Innovation #FutureOfWork #DigitalTransformation #Leadership #GenerativeAI #Accenture #TechLeadership #EngineeringManagement #RAndD #ProductDevelopment #TechTrends

posts.author: Joshua Reed
posts.headline: AI Infrastructure Engineer -- Member of Technical Staff at Andromeda
posts.text: I'm hiring, and so is the rest of Andromeda! Demand for AI compute is growing faster than any handful of providers can build. The GPUs exist, but they're scattered across hyperscalers, neoclouds and independent data centers, and they're hard to get when you need them. Andromeda is building the platform that makes all of that compute work as one, so model builders, research labs and inference teams get capacity when they need it. We want every spare electron doing useful work for AI. I'm leading the Platform team, and I'm growing the team by another 3-4 engineers, junior and senior. Platform is the part that makes it real. We turn racks of GPUs from anywhere into production-ready clusters with no human in the loop, then keep them healthy as they move from customer to customer. It's a hard systems problem, and it's at the center of the biggest infrastructure buildout of our lifetime. What I care about most is drive. I want people who chase a bug through four layers of the stack because they need to know why. People who own the outcome, not just the ticket, and who ship and then make it better. Skills can be taught. Hunger can't. If you've got that dog in you, I want to talk. posts.author: Marc Beierschoder
posts.headline: Most companies scale the wrong things. I fix that. | AI & Enterprise Transformation | Partner, Deloitte
posts.text: 𝗬𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗮𝘆, 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘁𝘀. 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆, 𝗼𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗻𝘀. I’m genuinely struggling to make sense of what’s happening in AI right now. In September, #OpenAI reported that its agents had produced a proposed solution to the famous Navier-Stokes problem in just 88 hours. Last week, it released another 722 mathematical manuscripts covering hundreds of research results. These are potentially extraordinary breakthroughs. Problems that challenged brilliant mathematicians for decades are suddenly being tackled by machines in days. And already, people are talking about #superintelligence. Even suggesting mathematicians should start looking for new careers. 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲? We heard the same argument about software engineers. AI would write all the code, so why keep hiring junior developers? I thought that was ridiculous then. I still do. And let’s not forget: producing a mathematical proof, independently validating it and replacing a mathematician are three very different things. The latest results still need scientific scrutiny. But there’s something else bothering me. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴. 𝗦𝗼 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀. #Anthropic is preparing for a potential IPO. OpenAI may eventually follow. Both need enormous amounts of capital, and every spectacular breakthrough strengthens their investment story. That doesn’t make the breakthroughs false. But it makes independent verification more important than ever. Andrew Karpathy recently argued that only around 5,000 people worldwide have access to the most advanced AI systems. If his estimate is even remotely accurate, the rest of humanity, including most AI experts, business leaders and policymakers, has never experienced what these systems are truly capable of. 𝗪𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗮 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗻. Perhaps he’s right. I work with AI every day and see remarkable capabilities alongside agents that still make elementary mistakes. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 - 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗼 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲? I don’t know how close we are to superintelligence. And I’m becoming increasingly skeptical of anyone who claims to know. But here’s what I’d really like to understand: 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 - 𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲? 𝘈𝘳𝘵 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘰 mad.charcoal

posts.text: We’re Hiring | Quality Assurance Intern / Software Tester About Bliss Apex Bliss Apex is a technology-focused company committed to building reliable, user-friendly, and high-quality digital experiences. We are looking for a detail-oriented and proactive candidate to join our team and help test our software projects end-to-end, ensuring quality, performance, and reliability before deployment. Role Overview As a Quality Assurance Intern / Software Tester, you will work closely with developers and the product team to identify issues, validate features, and ensure that our applications meet functional and quality standards. The ideal candidate should have a strong interest in software testing and a willingness to learn and work with real-world projects. Key Responsibilities - Perform manual, end-to-end, functional, and regression testing. - Test web and mobile applications to identify usability, functionality, and compatibility issues. - Create, execute, and maintain test cases and test scenarios. - Report, track, and verify bugs using Jira or similar task-tracking tools. - Perform API testing and validate API responses, status codes, and data. - Use tools such as Postman and Swagger for API testing and documentation. - Collaborate with developers to investigate, reproduce, and resolve defects. - Participate in the software development and testing lifecycle. - Ensure features meet requirements and quality standards before release. - Contribute to improving testing processes and documentation. Requirements - 0–1 year of experience in software testing; freshers are welcome to apply. - Basic understanding of manual, end-to-end, functional, and regression testing. - Knowledge of application testing for web and/or mobile applications. - Understanding of API testing concepts and experience or familiarity with Postman and Swagger. - Good understanding of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) and Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC). - Ability to write clear test cases, test scenarios, and bug reports. - Basic knowledge of React.js and Tailwind CSS is preferred. - Familiarity with Git/GitHub and version control. - Familiarity with Jira for task and bug tracking. - Strong analytical, problem-solving, communication, and teamwork skills. - Willingness to learn and work in a fast-paced environment. What We Offer - Hands-on experience with live software projects. - Exposure to real-world testing workflows and QA processes. - Practical experience with application and API testing. - Collaboration with developers and product teams. - Opportunities to improve your technical and professional skills. - A supportive and learning-focused work environment. - Potential growth opportunities based on performance. posts.author: Khyati Narwal
posts.headline: Helping software houses & agencies in DACH and the UK close engineering gaps in days, not months | B2B Sales & Partnerships at NetSet Software
posts.text: There are 64 remote junior engineering roles in Europe right now. And 2,230 remote mid-level ones. Same board, same week. Thirty-five times the difference. That gap explains something the shortage statistics do not. Remote hiring was supposed to widen the talent pool. What the numbers suggest is that it only widened it for people who were already experienced. Companies will let someone work from another country once they can be trusted to work without supervision. Before that, almost nobody will. So remote did not create new engineers. It redistributed the ones who already existed, and turned the competition for them from city-wide into continent-wide. The junior pipeline stayed exactly where it always was. Local, in an office, next to someone senior enough to teach. For scale: Germany has around 6,500 open engineering roles, about 1,000 of them remote. The UK has around 6,200, with roughly 1,100 remote. Fifteen to seventeen percent in both. Which means if you run a software house in either country, your options have not really changed. Compete across Europe for experienced people, or grow your own and absorb the senior time that costs. Most firms I speak to are doing neither deliberately. They are doing whichever one the last vacancy forced on them. Figures from Top Roles, this week. #Germany #UK #Softwareentwicklung #AgencyLife

posts.headline: Co-Founder @ Axiōma | Search partner to frontier AI & deep tech startups · Visit my website
posts.text: "Exceptional ML Engineers" is not a hiring brief. Neither is "we want cracked SWEs" or "we just want the best [title] you can find". Literally every AI startup wants that. But exceptional means different things to different companies. And even within the same company, it depends on the role. If you can't clearly explain what exceptional looks like for the role you're hiring for, how can you expect your talent team or external recruiters to find it? What backgrounds are relevant? What should they have built or achieved? What separates a good profile from one you'd immediately want to interview? And just as importantly, where are you willing to compromise? You won't always get the brief right on day one - that's fine. That's what calibration is for. But you've got to give the people running your search something concrete to work with. Otherwise, you're just asking them to guess what your hiring bar looks like.

posts.text: Let us do a hiring thought experiment. Candidate A: A junior developer with 1 year of experience who mastered AI agent workflows. They shipped 3 complete, working products in the last 6 months. Candidate B: A senior engineer with 12 years of experience who is still configuring ESLint, arguing about clean architecture patterns, and refactoring directory structures in Neovim. Five years ago, everyone picks Candidate B without hesitation. Today? Execution speed and shipping working software beat theoretical perfection every single week. If you are hiring tomorrow for a fast-moving product team, who do you actually hire? Candidate A or Candidate B? #softwareengineering #hiring #vibecoding #startups #techcareers

posts.text: In early 2026, US software job postings had about 15 senior roles for every entry-level one. Every senior engineer was a junior once. So where will the next seniors come from? On the surface, the news is good. US software developer postings are up almost 15% since late February 2025, while job postings overall fell 7%. But look at who those jobs are for. Between May 2025 and May 2026, 71% of the increase came from senior roles. In the first quarter of this year, 69.3% of software development postings were senior. Just 4.5% were entry-level. Payroll data points the same way. Stanford researchers found that employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is now 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with less-exposed work. Experienced workers show no such gap. The researchers call this an early signal, not proof that AI is the cause. I understand why it's happening. AI agents now do a lot of what we used to hand to juniors: the boilerplate, the first version of a component, the small bug fix. But juniors never learned from those tasks because the tasks were important. They learned because doing them, and having them reviewed, is how judgment gets built. And judgment is exactly what AI-written code needs. Someone has to notice when it's wrong. That skill takes years, and it starts at entry level. Not every company is pulling back. In February, IBM said it would triple its entry-level hiring in the US this year, with junior developers spending less time on routine coding and more time with customers. If you're early in your career, here's what I'd focus on: → Learn to read and review code, not just write it. Checking AI output is part of the job now. → Ship one real thing end to end, and be ready to explain every decision in it. → Get good at what AI is weak at: understanding the user, asking what the requirement really is, and debugging on a real device. And if you're senior: take the junior. Review their code like it matters. Someone did that for us. If you hire engineers: are you still hiring juniors? What changed in how you hire them? Sources: Indeed Hiring Lab (Jul 2026), Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Aug 2026), Bloomberg (Feb 2026). #SoftwareEngineering #AI #Hiring #CareerAdvice #FutureOfWork

posts.text: Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code, called coding "largely solved" in February. Developer job postings are up nearly 15% since Claude Code launched. So who's getting hired? Senior roles took 71% of the rise in the year to May. Early-career developer employment is down 20%. Firms still need developers to oversee what the AI writes. The job moved up, from typing code to judging it, and that's the bit I'm excited about. The catch sits in that 20%. The same economist: "Today's entry-level talent becomes tomorrow's senior experts." Coding solved, and still hiring. Would you hire a junior developer this year?

posts.text: 🎓 FINAL-YEAR STUDENTS: If you graduate in 2027, don’t choose your career based only on what’s trending. A better question is: “What can I demonstrate to an employer by graduation?” Here’s a practical way to decide your next 6 months: 1️⃣ Pick 2 roles to compare, not 10. Examples: software developer vs data analyst, QA engineer vs cloud support, or digital marketing vs business development. 2️⃣ Read 15–20 real job descriptions for each role. Track repeated skills, tools, degree requirements, location and whether freshers are accepted. Don’t assume every “high-demand” skill creates entry-level jobs. 3️⃣ Choose the role where your interest overlaps with realistic requirements and the skills you can build. 4️⃣ Build one project that proves those skills. Document the problem, your contribution, decisions, result and what you learned. 5️⃣ Recheck job descriptions every month. Hiring needs can change before your graduation. The goal isn’t to predict every job in 2027. It’s to make a decision based on evidence instead of social-media hype. 👇 Final-year students: Which two career paths are you currently comparing? Comment them. I’ll help you identify what to check before choosing. posts.text: You want to build an app? Oya, calm down first! 😂 Before you call your guy that knows React, or start asking ChatGPT to generate code, there are things you need to understand. Because building software is not just: "Give me the design." "Write the code." "Deploy am." "Collect money." 💰 If na so e easy, every WhatsApp group for Nigeria for don get one billionaire tech founder. 😂 Over the next 7 days, I'll be breaking down the major stages of software development, from the moment you get an idea to the day users start complaining that something is not working. 🤣 Here is what we'll cover: 📌 Day 1: Requirements Gathering. What problem are we solving? 📌 Day 2: Planning and Documentation. Who does what, when, and how? 📌 Day 3: Product Design and UX. Before coding starts, let's draw the map. 📌 Day 4: Development. Frontend, backend, databases, and DevOps. 📌 Day 5: Security. Because "Nobody will hack us" is not a security strategy. 😭 📌 Day 6: Testing and Deployment. Let's find the wahala before the users do. 📌 Day 7: Maintenance and Iteration. Launching is not the finish line. Whether you're a founder with an idea, a junior developer, a designer, or someone curious about tech, this series is for you. My goal is simple: help you understand what it actually takes to turn an idea into working software. Let's start with one question: If you had ₦10 million to build an app today, would you start by hiring developers or by understanding the problem you want to solve? posts.headline: Founder & CEO of Strativa Web Solution | Selify Nigeria | Software Developer | Building E-commerce and real-world digital products
posts.text: A website without SEO is like opening a beautiful shop in a place nobody knows exists. This one is for the decision-makers in business CEOs, Business Development Managers, HR Managers, Heads of Departments, and business owners. If you’re not in any of these categories, you might want to scroll to the next post. 😊 Just kidding Pull up a chair and stay with me. You’re about to learn something strategic. Let me ask you a simple question. What is the point of having a business website if your potential customers can’t find it? Having a website is a great step towards building your business online. But hiring a developer to build your website and make it live is only the beginning. Here’s where many businesses miss a crucial piece of the puzzle SEO (Search Engine Optimisation). And yes, I’ll say it again. SEO! When hiring a professional to build your website or develop custom business software, don't focus only on the design, features, and delivery timeline. Ask questions about how the solution will help your business get discovered online, where applicable. A website should do more than look good. It should be built with visibility, usability, and business goals in mind. Think about it. You’ve owned a website for five years. Every year, you renew your domain and pay for hosting, but your website has generated no meaningful enquiries, leads, or sales. Of course, not every website is designed to generate direct sales. Some serve other purposes. But if your website is meant to attract customers and support business growth, shouldn't it be contributing to those goals? A website that nobody can find is missing a major part of its potential. This is why I believe website development and SEO should work together from the start, not be treated as completely separate projects. And the opportunity goes beyond traditional search engines. As more people use AI-powered platforms to discover businesses, products, and services, it's also worth considering how your website's content and structure can help these platforms understand your business and its expertise. That’s the approach I bring to my work. I BUILD. I OPTIMISE. I HELP BUSINESSES IMPROVE THEIR ONLINE VISIBILITY. My goal is not just to help you put a website online, but to help you build a stronger digital presence that supports your business objectives. So, if your business has a website that isn't delivering the value you expected, perhaps it's time to look beyond the design and ask the right questions. Let's talk. Send me a message, and let's explore how to make your website work harder for your business.

posts.text: I was waiting a long time to make a post with a new offer in it. Not this time, but here’s what happened instead. 😄 I recently went through the hiring processes at Hevo Data, mthree and Infosys. Each one took me further than I expected and showed me something different about where I stand. Hevo Data (SDE-1, Backend) The role was a great fit and the pay was really good, so this was one I wanted badly. Online assessment with 6 questions. A 2-hour LLD round (a Ride Sharing Application). LLD was new to me, I learned it in a hurry, and I cleared it in C++, which is not the easiest language for it.cleared it Stopped at the manager round, where maybe team fit ig was not there with me, I was almost there. mthree Assessment, then a group discussion where we had to speak on AI. Technical round with 2 Java questions plus SQL. Java was something I had learned recently, and I got through it. I cleared every round but ended up on the waitlist because of limited vacancies. Infosys Round 1 was an online DSA exam, and I solved the questions well enough to move forward. Round 2 was an offline DSA exam in Delhi. I solved it and earned a place in the L1 interview. I cleared the L1 interview and reached the final round. There, the questions were on system design, HLD and the architecture of my own projects. Time was tight, and it showed me how deep I need to go on design decisions, trade-offs and scaling. What I’m taking from this I’m not blaming the companies. The things in my control are my preparation and how I show up, and that is where I’m working. Know your projects at the architecture level. Be ready to explain why you built them the way you did, what the HLD looks like and how they would scale. Time management in interviews is a skill. I’m practicing it with timed mock sessions. Behavioral preparation matters as much as technical preparation. Explaining my decisions and trade-offs clearly is the next thing I’m improving. Learning a new language or topic fast, as I did with Java and LLD, works. It just needs to be paired with depth. Beyond the prep Outside of interviews, I’ve been going to the gym, sleeping properly, keeping a steady routine and updating my skills and resume. All of it helped a lot more than I expected, and it keeps me sharp and calm through the waiting. There has been a bit of luck and a bit of bad luck along the way, but I’m in a good place. I enjoyed these processes, I’m clear on what to improve, and I’m hopeful that something good comes soon. #InterviewExperience #HevoData #mthree #Infosys #SoftwareEngineering #SystemDesign #LowLevelDesign

posts.author: Harish Kumar V
posts.headline: Building "Be Practical" - On a Mission to Create Future Ready Workforce | Founder @Yugyantra Technologies Pvt Ltd
posts.text: Every company wants AI talent. Almost none of them want to build it. Naukri's September data makes this painfully clear: → AI/ML hiring: +20% → Overall white-collar hiring: +1% → Freshers (0–3 yrs): +1% That 20x gap isn't a blip. It's a signal about how the market now works. Look at who's actually winning: Experience Growth 0–3 years +1% 4–7 years −2% 8–12 years +5% 13–15 years +7% 16+ years +5% Mid-level is shrinking. Senior is growing. Entry-level is flat. The market is hollowing out from the middle and rewarding the top. And look at where the growth is: ✅ AI/ML +20% ✅ Auto +11% ✅ BPO/ITES +4% ❌ IT/Software Services −4% ❌ Hospitality −11% ❌ Telecom −12% ❌ Education −18% The irony is brutal: AI is booming inside an IT sector that's shrinking. Same industry, opposite trajectories. The generic developer role is being automated; the AI specialist role is being created. What this actually means: 1. "Learn AI" isn't advice anymore—it's table stakes. The +20% is real, but it's concentrated in people who can build, not people who can talk about AI. This is the same point HCLTech made: exposure ≠ employability. 2. The experience ladder is broken. If 4–7 years is shrinking and 16+ is growing, the rungs in the middle are missing. That's a structural problem companies will feel in a decade. 3. Geography is diversifying. Udaipur +19%, Chandigarh +18%, Amritsar +13%. Meanwhile Delhi-NCR and Mumbai both fell 6%. The old "move to Bengaluru" playbook is outdated. The honest takeaway for freshers: The market isn't closed. It's selective. And "selective" means it rewards specificity, demonstrable skill, and being in the right sector—not a degree and a hope.

posts.author: Chatresh Consultants
posts.text: The Education Gap & the Unspoken Realities of Junior Tech Hiring Why do we treat software engineering education like memorising state capitals? Memorise the syntax. Answer 30 multiple-choice questions. Submit a neat, isolated solo coursework assignment. Get an 'A'. Then that same graduate walks into their very first technical interview or probationary sprint, and the engineering lead asks: • “Walk me through how you resolve a rebase conflict on a team branch.” • “How would you trace an unhandled promise rejection crashing this microservice?” • “Explain the database locking trade-off in your latest project.” Silence. Here is the inconvenient truth that academic curricula and 12-week online video bootcamps rarely address: writing new code is only about 30% of a working software engineer’s job. The other 70% is messy, unpredictable, and social: 1. Digging through legacy code with zero documentation. 2. Formulating the exact technical question to ask when you've been blocked for 45 minutes. 3. Defending design decisions during an architecture review without taking criticism personally. 4. Structuring Pull Requests so your senior colleagues don't reject your branch on sight. You cannot absorb that through passive screen time. Watching an instructor code in a pre-recorded sandbox gives the illusion of competence—until you open an empty terminal on your own machine and nothing works. At the LUYSK (Level Up Your Skills-learning arm of Chatresh Consultants) center in Sevenoaks, Kent, we built a learning model that completely strips out the classroom lecture. When students walk through our doors, they don’t sit in rows looking at slides. They log into a dedicated dual-monitor workstation inside an active engineering room. They join a real morning standup. They take on blocker tickets, whiteboard system data flows with senior developers who build real enterprise systems, and learn the discipline of writing production-grade code. If you want someone to learn how to play football, you don’t keep them in a lecture hall reading the official rulebook. You give them boots and put them on the pitch. Tech education should work the exact same way. To the engineering managers and developers reading this: what was the single biggest shock you faced during your first month working in a real engineering team? posts.text: I put a sign on a wall offering a session on hiring or looking for a job At one point, around 9 people were sitting with me This was during the #unconference part at the t3 cto summit - Software Engineering Leadership last Friday, after my Human API roundtable (shout out to Manjuri) So people brought their questions or ideas or thoughts related to Hiring and / or Job Searches and then we just went through them...it was a lot of: "I will need to make assumptions here" and "Please allow me to simply rapid fire ideas, to save time" - on my part (normally I would have asked them waaaay more questions 👀 It felt like a continuous coaching session 😆 for over 2.5h, and I realised it lasted so long when I stood up and everything in my body hurt 🤭 I loved EVERY minute or it And I realised how much I had missed being around tech and senior people 😫 I spent 16 years in tech or specialist engineering. Spending time again with engineering leaders, founders and people between roles brings me closer to the work I am really good at My roundtable surfaced some questions (another post abt this): • How do you assess technical judgement when candidates use AI? • How do you develop junior engineers when their starting tasks disappear? • How do you recognise good performance when output is easier to produce? Then the unconference brought the conversation directly to individual hiring and career decisions We need more time listening outside our own professional circles! Before producing another hiring framework, workshop or piece of content, ask an <insert profession> leader what they are struggling to assess. Ask someone looking for work where the process loses them Their answers should shape our work, not more of the "wanna be" overnight "gurus" on LinkedIn, some of which gained notoriety because you see their face often (yes, mine included perhaps), and not because they ever did the job properly - but speak to the Re-Le-Vaaaant people!!! Pretty please 🙏 Thank you, Greg Fawson, for having me back. More of this, please 😍

posts.author: Prithviraj Manoharlal Tiwari
posts.headline: ​SITPUNE
posts.text: We need an honest discussion about the current math facing engineering graduates. ​For the past many years where large service firms absorbed entire graduating classes has fundamentally shifted. Routine coding is getting automated, entry-level hiring has contracted, and yet degrees still cost ₹15–25 lakhs across tuition and living expenses. Meanwhile, students spend the majority of their daily bandwidth complying with statutory attendance requirements, assignment submissions, and educational institutions' administrative workings. ​Telling everyone to simply pivot into DevOps, Forward Deployed Engineering, or advanced software architecture is unrealistic. Those roles demand deep specialization, not surface-level certificates. ​If you are a student right now, the time for passive waiting is gone. You essentially have three realistic choices: ​Self-Audit for the Top Tier: Be completely honest with your technical aptitude. If you have the drive and capability to compete at the highest level, commit fully. Go deep into distributed systems, low-level architecture, or specialized domains so you stand out as a specialized engineer for modern engineering teams. ​Embrace the MSME & Early Startup Path: If you realize you fit a more conventional profile, drop the stigma around smaller businesses, MSMEs, operations, and early-stage startups. The initial paycheck will likely be modest, but the hands-on exposure, rapid ownership, and practical problem-solving skills you gain offer a far better long-term upside than waiting for an MNC drive that may never come. ​Ignore the Shift and Proceed as Usual: If you prefer to stick to conventional advice, wait out the market, or bet on legacy placement patterns, that is entirely your prerogative. No judgment—sincerely, good luck with your path. ​The worst place to be right now is in the middle: carrying heavy expectations without a clear strategy.

posts.text: Some of Germany’s most demanding AI engineering challenges happen outside the chatbot. Einige der anspruchsvollsten KI-Engineering-Aufgaben in Deutschland liegen außerhalb von Chatbots… Autonomous mobility is one example. Berlin based Motor Ai is developing Level 4 autonomous driving technology. Its Robotics Software Integration Engineer vacancy offers an interesting view of the work behind that ambition. C++. Linux. ROS2. Sensor interfaces. Build pipelines. Systems integration. The role includes reviewing critical code, resolving interface mismatches and coordinating software releases. These are the details that make an intelligent system work as a whole. The software needs to communicate with sensors. Different components need to work together. Changes need to be reviewed. And engineers need to understand how a problem in one part of the system affects another. From a recruitment perspective, this connects disciplines that are often assessed separately: → C++ Software Engineering → Robotics → ROS2 → Embedded Systems → Sensor Integration → CI/CD → Systems Engineering The wider field also depends on testing and safety expertise. That doesn’t mean one engineer needs to master every discipline. It means hiring teams need to understand where someone can take responsibility. Can they integrate software with hardware? Diagnose problems across components? Help deliver dependable releases? I think this is a particularly interesting opportunity for Germany’s industrial and automotive engineering talent. Experience with physical systems could become increasingly valuable as AI moves into operational environments. The strongest candidate may be someone who understands both the intelligence and the engineering surrounding it. Do you think Germany’s industrial engineering background gives it an advantage in physical AI? #PhysicalAI #Robotics #AutonomousDriving #AIEngineering #EmbeddedSystems #Germany #MachineLearning #TechRecruitment #MAMGruppe #Deutschland #KI #Marktupdate

posts.headline: Founder & CTO @ AUREM · Building AI that ships code not just suggests it.
posts.text: "Only developers can maintain software." That belief is about to get old. Most non-technical founders who build with Lovable, Bolt, Replit or v0 hit the same wall after launch: the demo worked, something breaks, and they have no idea why. They either wait on a freelancer or go back into the builder and hope. Here's what we built instead. Inside ORA, 3 separate AI engineers each independently write a fix for your bug. A 4th model reviews all 3 and picks the best one. Only then does it get saved to your actual GitHub repo — nothing ships without that review, and nothing ships without your approval either. You never read a line of code. You just describe what's wrong in plain English. The one requirement: your app's code needs to be on GitHub. Lovable, Bolt, Replit and v0 all have a GitHub sync — turn it on, connect it to ORA, and you can run your own app without hiring an engineer. Starter plan is $9/month. If you've built something with AI and it's started acting up, I'd genuinely like to hear what broke. posts.author: Sai Krishna Garrepalli, PMP®
posts.headline: Connecting Science, Business and AI to Create Real-World Impact | Founder, PiBTC and LSCI | Supporting Leaders, Companies and Future Talent
posts.text: Most companies chase the newest tool. The best companies master approaches. Over years across Pharma, MedTech, and Healthcare, I keep seeing the same mistake. Organizations ask: Should we implement AI? Should we adopt Lean? Should we buy this software? Wrong questions. The most successful organizations ask something entirely different. What approach will help us consistently deliver better outcomes? Let us look at what actually works in the real world. Case 1: GE and Six Sigma. When Jack Welch scaled Six Sigma, it was never just a quality initiative. It became an operating system. Decisions became data driven. Improvement stopped being a project and became the culture. Case 2: Medtronic in Hyderabad. Building a massive R&D footprint wasn't just about hiring smart engineers. It required structured processes that enable innovation at scale. Without process discipline, great tech just creates expensive noise. Case 3: Siemens Healthineers. Colocating manufacturing and R&D in Bengaluru to bring products to market faster. That is classic process thinking. Optimize the entire value stream, not just isolated departments. Case 4: Pharma Quality Culture. The shift from reactive quality control to proactive quality culture. Because preventing a defect always beats fixing one after it hits the market. Here is what leaders eventually realize. Technology changes constantly. Approaches endure. If you want to advance fast in Life Sciences and MedTech, stop collecting tools and certificates. Master the fundamentals: Process thinking Root cause analysis Systems design Continuous improvement Change leadership Because the framework that actually works is simple: Problem first. Process second. People third. Technology last. Looking back at your career, what had the bigger impact on your growth? A specific tool or software? Or a problem solving approach that completely changed how you think? Drop your thoughts below. #LifeSciences #Pharma #MedTech #SixSigma #Lean #ContinuousImprovement #Leadership #Healthcare #Strategy

posts.headline: Visit website
posts.text: When we hire developers today, "how fast can you write code?" is no longer the question that matters most. AI tools can generate a working function in seconds. What they can't do is decide whether that function should exist at all. So here is what we pay closer attention to now: → Can you read code you didn't write? Most real work is understanding an existing system, not starting fresh. Reviewing AI-generated code is the same skill. → Do you ask about the requirement before the solution? The best candidates ask "who uses this and what problem does it solve?" before choosing a framework. → Can you explain a trade-off in plain language? Our clients are clinic owners, school administrators and founders. If you can't explain why something takes two weeks, the project gets harder for everyone. → Do you know when something is wrong? Spotting a security gap, a slow query or a missing edge case is worth more than writing extra lines. → Do you take ownership after launch? Software lives for years. The people who care about how it behaves in month six are the ones we want on the team. For junior developers, this is good news. You don't need to know every tool. You need to understand problems clearly, keep learning, and get comfortable reviewing and testing, not just generating. Developers and hiring managers: what skill do you think matters more now than it did five years ago? #SoftwareDevelopment #Hiring #DeveloperCareers #TechTeams #AI

posts.headline: Senior Software Development Engineer at Be10x
posts.text: Everyone is saying software engineering is finished. But one perspective from a Google Engineering Manager with nearly 20 years in tech suggests that what’s really changing is the role of the engineer—not the need for engineers. AI isn't replacing software engineers overnight. It is changing what engineers need to be good at. 1. Coding is changing, not disappearing The value is shifting toward problem-solving, architecture, edge cases, and understanding the customer. 2. We're entering the agentic era AI can now handle increasingly complex tasks, but giving it a completely new real-world problem and expecting it to independently understand context and own the outcome is still a much higher bar. 3. Fresher hiring will get harder "I know Java + LeetCode" won't be enough. Engineers will need to show they can build with AI, question its output, and take ownership of what ships. 4. CS fundamentals still matter Focus on: → DSA → OS & Networks → Distributed Systems → System Design → Problem Solving 5. Interviews will evolve Expect more questions like: → Debug AI-generated code → Find security issues → Scale a system → Review an AI solution The question shifts from "Can you write code?" to "Can you judge code?" 6. Teams won't necessarily shrink dramatically The same team may simply become far more productive, with more emphasis on senior-level thinking and decision-making. 7. Human value moves toward judgment Business context. Trade-offs. Collaboration. Ownership. When production breaks, someone still needs to understand the problem and own the fix. 8. Learn fundamentals before relying on AI Code without AI first. Understand how systems work. Then use AI aggressively—as a partner, not a replacement for understanding. 9. If you learn only 3 things this year: → Agentic workflows → Systems + data architecture → Business understanding The future of software engineering may not be about writing less code. posts.author: Hasnat Awan, AMIMechE
posts.headline: Graduate Mechanical Engineer at Southern Water
posts.text: Graduate jobs aren’t simply “disappearing because of AI” — but the skills employers expect from graduates are changing fast. A UK government analysis published this year found that overall UK hiring was 14% lower year-on-year in April 2026. Among the entry-level occupations it tracked, Accountant roles were down 29% and Software Engineer roles were down 27%. In total, 30 of the 38 entry-level occupations analysed had seen hiring decline. That sounds worrying — especially if you are graduating into tech, finance or another competitive professional field. But the picture is more complicated than “AI has taken the graduate jobs.” The Institute of Student Employers’ 2026 research found that 87% of employers expect AI to reshape graduate and apprentice roles over the next three years. Importantly, employers generally expect roles to be changed rather than simply replaced. And new Skills England research published in October shows that demand still exists in important areas: software development, IT business analysis and several engineering occupations appear repeatedly as priority skills across UK growth sectors. In digital and technology, around 68% of priority occupations are considered to be in critical or elevated demand, while the equivalent figure in financial services is around 70%. So what is changing? Employers increasingly want graduates who can work beyond routine tasks. In tech, AI is shifting value towards verification, judgement and communication; in finance, it is transforming analytics, fraud detection and risk; and engineering demand remains strong across areas such as clean energy, advanced manufacturing and defence. The goal is not simply to become an “AI expert” — it is to combine your profession with practical AI literacy and strong human judgement. For international graduates, this matters even more because sponsorship adds another filter to an already competitive market. Your application needs to show what you can contribute, not just that you have a degree and need sponsorship. Whether you are in finance, software or engineering, combine your technical skills with data, AI literacy, problem-solving and communication. And remember: a government “priority occupation” is not automatically sponsorable immigration eligibility still needs to be checked separately. My takeaway for graduates entering the 2026/27 market is simple: don’t try to compete with AI at the repetitive tasks it can increasingly perform. Build the skills that make you valuable alongside it judgement, verification, problem-solving, technical depth, communication and the ability to apply technology to real business problems. Sources: Skills England Annual Skills Report and Sector Skills Needs Assessments 2026 #GraduateJobs #InternationalGraduates #InternationalStudents #EngineeringJobs #FinanceCareers #TechCareers #ArtificialIntelligence #VisaSponsorship #UKJobs #GraduateCareers

posts.headline: Experienced technologist. AI Pragmatist | Web3 | E-Commerce | Angel Investor
posts.text: Last month, 24th August. I was on a panel at DevOps Summit Singapore. And the topic: the socio-technical architecture of software-enabled organisations. The point I kept coming back to was this. With AI writing more of the code, the engineer's job moves to specification, verification and orchestration, a point that my fellow panelist Abhik Roychoudhury mentioned when he said that verification and validation is now more important than ever. In my team at Mighty Jaxx, that is already how we work, from using MCP servers for Figma to Shopify code to QA agents. But the code was never the hard part. Someone still has to say exactly what we want, and check that what comes back is correct. That also raises a question which I care about: where do junior engineers learn if AI takes the entry-level tasks? I don't have a full answer yet. But hiring, mentoring and giving interns real work is a good place to start. And interns are expected to be given knottier problems to solve much sooner and the acceleration along the learning curve will accelerate. Now is in fact, a great time to be a software developer as demand will outpace supply It was a session of good questions and great conversations. Thanks to everyone who came by to chat after the session. And thanks to my panel host Sergiu Bodiu and my fellow panelists Albert Xu Ray Booysen and Abhik Roychoudhury for a great discussion. #DevOpsSummitSG #DevOps #AI #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text: Companies are opening more roles, not fewer. If AI were replacing engineers, hiring activity would be dropping, but the demand for developer talent remains active. If anyone can build software with AI, what exactly are companies hiring developers for? AI makes writing code fast, letting teams spin up basic templates and small features in seconds. But writing more code does not equal a working system. When teams rely on AI to write code without careful checking, they get stuck with messy code, hidden bugs, and serious security risks. This is why companies keep hiring developers. They are not looking for someone to type out basic code—AI already does that. They need engineers who understand how different systems connect, how to keep data secure, and how to fix complex problems when things break down. Writing code is cheap now. Good engineering judgment is what companies are actually paying for. #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechHiring #BackendDevelopment #TechLeadership
